episode_title: E-Bike and E-Scooter Laws and Liability

segment_1.topic_phrase: why an electric bike or scooter leaves you with no coverage at all
segment_1.setup: I'm **{{INTERVIEWER}}**, and today we're on something almost nobody looks into until they need it. If you ride an electric bike or a scooter in Florida, you're outside the insurance system every driver takes for granted, and almost nobody knows that.
segment_1.credential: **{{ATTORNEY}}**, your firm handles a wide range of injury work, and a lot of it involves people who weren't in a car at all.
segment_1.prompt: Someone was just knocked off a scooter by a car. Lay out what's different about their situation. And if you've a real-world example, take us through it.

attributes.detail: The percentage, whether it rises if you file suit, who pays to have a failed part examined, and what happens if you lose.

questions.q: You were on an e-bike or a scooter in Stuart. What does Florida law actually call it?

bullets.label: It's the first question in the case
bullets.detail: an electric bike, a scooter and a moped are three different things in Florida, and which one you were on decides the coverage.

bullets.label: An e-bike is treated like a bicycle
bullets.detail: same rights on the road, same duties, and that's where the rules come from.

bullets.label: A scooter sits in its own category
bullets.detail: Florida law says it'sn't a motor vehicle, and that changes everything about coverage.

questions.q: What are the three classes of e-bike in Florida, and why do they matter?

bullets.label: Class one and two stop at twenty
bullets.detail: one helps only while you pedal, the other has a throttle, and both cut out at twenty miles an hour.

bullets.label: Class three goes to twenty-eight
bullets.detail: faster, more crash energy, tighter rules about who can ride it and where.

bullets.label: The class is what the fight is about
bullets.detail: it sets where you were allowed to ride and how fast you were allowed to go.

questions.q: Does a rented scooter work differently from your own around Stuart?

bullets.label: The state rules are the same
bullets.detail: what changes is the paperwork you agreed to when you unlocked it.

bullets.label: The rental terms are the fine print
bullets.detail: app coverage tends to carry low limits and exclusions people never read.

bullets.label: How it shows up here
bullets.detail: most riding here's on somebody's own bike rather than a rental, so the coverage you're looking for is usually a policy on a car in that household.

questions.q: Where can you legally ride one in Stuart and across the Treasure Coast?

bullets.label: The road and the bike lane
bullets.detail: an e-bike belongs where a bicycle belongs, which is the road or the bike lane, not the sidewalk in most places.

bullets.label: Sidewalks are where it changes
bullets.detail: the sidewalk rule is set town by town, so check the rule for the town you actually ride in.

bullets.label: Where it goes wrong here
bullets.detail: US 1 and Kanner Highway are built for speed with no real place for two wheels, and A1A puts riders alongside beach traffic at crossings that are a long way apart.

questions.q: Does Florida make you wear a helmet on one of these?

bullets.label: Only under sixteen
bullets.detail: the requirement is an age rule, and above it the choice is yours.

bullets.label: Not wearing one is still used
bullets.detail: it'sn't a violation, but the other side will raise it against a head injury claim anyway.

bullets.label: It doesn't end the claim
bullets.detail: the other side can argue it and a jury can reduce what you recover, but it doesn't take away your right to bring the claim.

questions.q: Do you need a license, registration or insurance to ride one in Florida?

bullets.label: You don't register one like a car
bullets.detail: and that's exactly why no injury coverage comes attached to it.

bullets.label: That's the trap
bullets.detail: people assume something covers them the way a car policy does, and nothing does.

bullets.label: Check before you need to
bullets.detail: the coverage question has an answer, and finding it out after a crash is the expensive way.

questions.q: If a car hits you on a scooter, does your own injury coverage apply?

bullets.label: Not the way you would expect
bullets.detail: no-fault coverage is tied to motor vehicles, and a scooter isn't one, so nothing follows the scooter itself.

bullets.label: So nothing pays the first bills
bullets.detail: the emergency room bill shows up and there's no coverage behind it, and around here a serious injury means a transfer out of the county, which is a second bill on top of the first.

bullets.label: It sends the claim elsewhere
bullets.detail: straight to the driver who hit you and to your own uninsured coverage.

questions.q: A scooter isn't a motor vehicle under Florida law. Why does that one fact control the whole claim?

bullets.label: It takes away the automatic coverage
bullets.detail: with a car, something pays your first bills no matter who caused the crash, and on a scooter nothing does.

bullets.label: Fault becomes everything
bullets.detail: with nothing paying automatically, proving the driver caused it's the only route.

bullets.label: It changes the urgency
bullets.detail: the evidence has to be locked down immediately, because there's no coverage sitting there paying while anyone works it out.

questions.q: If you own a car, can you still use that policy after a scooter crash in Stuart?

bullets.label: Often yes, and people never ask
bullets.detail: your own car policy can still cover you even though you were nowhere near the car, and around here most riders do own one.

bullets.label: A relative's policy can count too
bullets.detail: somebody in the same household with coverage may bring you inside it.

bullets.label: Bring every policy
bullets.detail: the declarations page, the summary sheet at the front, from every car in the house, and that's the first thing to gather.

questions.q: When your own coverage doesn't apply, whose insurance actually pays?

bullets.label: The driver who hit you, first
bullets.detail: their liability coverage is the main route, and in Florida that coverage is optional.

bullets.label: Then your own uninsured coverage
bullets.detail: which is why it matters far more to a rider than to a driver.

bullets.label: Then the others in the chain
bullets.detail: whoever built it if a part failed, and the county or the city if the road itself was the problem, and a claim against a government carries a much shorter deadline.
